question: What is SwiftUI and how does it differ from UIKit?
answer:
SwiftUI is Apple's declarative UI framework, introduced in iOS 13 (2019). You describe what the UI should look like for a given state; the framework diffs and applies changes.

Key differences vs UIKit:
• Declarative — `var body: some View` returns a view tree; UIKit was imperative (build, then mutate UIViews).
• Single source of truth — state drives rendering; SwiftUI invalidates and re-runs `body` when state changes.
• Composition — small views combine into bigger ones; modifiers are values that transform a view.
• Cross-platform — same code runs on iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS, visionOS.
• View is a value type (struct), recreated cheaply on every body invocation. UIView was a reference type.

question: Explain stack containers in SwiftUI: VStack, HStack, ZStack, LazyVStack/HStack.
answer:
Stacks are how SwiftUI lays out children along an axis, and picking one is mostly a question of direction plus whether the content is long enough to need laziness.

• VStack — children top to bottom. Takes `alignment` (horizontal) and `spacing`.
• HStack — children left to right. Takes `alignment` (vertical) and `spacing`.
• ZStack — children back to front along the Z axis, aligned to a single `alignment` point.
• LazyVStack / LazyHStack — same layout, but children are only created as they approach the viewport. They belong inside a ScrollView; on their own they have no scrolling.
• Grid — a real two-dimensional layout with `GridRow`, where columns line up across rows. LazyVGrid and LazyHGrid are the scrolling, item-count-driven alternatives.

A non-lazy stack sizes itself by asking every child, so a VStack of 10,000 rows builds 10,000 views before the first one appears. That is the whole reason the lazy variants exist — and also why a LazyVStack cannot centre its content, since it does not know its own height yet.

`Spacer()` is a low-priority flexible view that pushes siblings apart, and layout priority breaks ties when the parent cannot satisfy everyone. When stacks stop being enough, the `Layout` protocol lets you write a custom container, and `ViewThatFits` picks the first child that fits.

question: How do view modifiers work in SwiftUI?
answer:
A modifier is a method on View that returns a new view wrapping the original with extra behavior (padding, background, foreground, gesture). Modifiers compose left-to-right; order matters.

Key points:
• Each modifier returns `some View` — the result is a new struct, not a mutated view.
• Order changes layout: `.padding().background(.red)` differs from `.background(.red).padding()` — the former adds red around content+padding, the latter pads then puts red behind only content.
• Custom modifiers via `ViewModifier` protocol or extension on View.
• Some modifiers are environment-aware (e.g. `.font` reads from environment).

question: How does navigation work in SwiftUI? NavigationStack and NavigationSplitView.
answer:
SwiftUI navigation is state-driven: you push by appending a value to a path, not by calling a method on a navigation controller.

• NavigationStack — push and pop navigation. `NavigationStack(path: $path)` binds either a typed array of route values or a `NavigationPath` for heterogeneous routes. Appending pushes, removing pops, `path.removeAll()` pops to root.
• NavigationSplitView — two- or three-column sidebar / content / detail layout for iPad, Mac and visionOS, which collapses to a plain stack automatically on iPhone.
• `.navigationDestination(for:)` registers a route type, and `NavigationLink(value:)` supplies a value of that type. The two are matched by type, which is what decouples the link from the destination.

`NavigationView` and `NavigationLink(destination:)` have been deprecated since iOS 16 and should not appear in new code.

Two things that bite people:
• `.navigationDestination` must be inside the stack's content and must not be inside a lazy container — put it on the List, not on a row, or the modifier is never registered and the push silently does nothing.
• Because the path is just data, deep linking and state restoration are ordinary array operations. Decode a URL into `[Route]`, assign it, and the whole stack appears — no imperative sequence of pushes, and no timing bugs.

question: How do you build a List in SwiftUI, and why does row identity matter?
answer:
A List gives you a scrolling, platform-styled container with separators, selection, swipe actions and pull-to-refresh for the cost of one view, and `ForEach` fills it from a collection.

The pieces:
• List — the container. `.listStyle(.plain / .insetGrouped / .sidebar)` picks the look.
• ForEach — generates one view per element. Works inside List, VStack and LazyVStack alike.
• Section — groups rows under an optional header and footer.
• Row-level modifiers — `.swipeActions(edge:)`, `.listRowSeparator`, `.listRowBackground`, `.contextMenu`.
• List-level modifiers — `.searchable(text:)`, `.refreshable { await ... }`, `.moveDisabled`, and `List(selection:)` for single or multiple selection.

Identity is the part people get wrong. SwiftUI diffs the old and new element lists by identity, and that identity decides which view keeps its state, which row animates from where, and whether the scroll position survives a reload. Conform your model to `Identifiable` with a stable id from your data — a database id or a UUID stored on the model.

The classic bug is `ForEach(items, id: \.self)` on a value type, or an `id` derived from the array index. Both make identity change whenever the content or the order changes, so rows lose their state, animations jump, and in-flight edits get reattached to the wrong row.

For a very long list, prefer `List` over `ScrollView` + `LazyVStack`: List already reuses rows, whereas a LazyVStack creates every row it has scrolled past and keeps it.

question: How do you write SwiftUI previews for a view with several states or a service dependency?
answer:
Previews render a view inside Xcode without launching the app, which turns the iteration loop from a build-and-navigate into a couple of seconds.

The API is the `#Preview` macro; `PreviewProvider` is the older form you will still meet in existing code. Add `@Previewable` to a `@State` declaration inside a `#Preview` when the view needs a live binding to drive.

How to make previews earn their keep:
• One preview per state that has its own layout risk — loading, empty, error, one item, many items, longest realistic string.
• Cover the environment axes that break layouts: `.preferredColorScheme(.dark)`, `.environment(\.dynamicTypeSize, .accessibility1)`, `.environment(\.layoutDirection, .rightToLeft)`.
• Keep sample data in a factory next to the model (`User.preview`) rather than inlining a fixture in every preview.
• Inject a fake service so the preview never touches the network. For an `@Observable` dependency that means `.environment(MockService())`; for a legacy `ObservableObject` it is still `.environmentObject(...)`.
• Give each preview a name (`#Preview("Empty state")`) — the names are how you navigate the canvas once there are six of them.

A preview that cannot be created without a network call, a database, or a logged-in session is telling you the view knows too much. Push the dependency out behind a protocol and the preview becomes trivial — which is why previews are a design pressure, not just a viewer.
